WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- While nearly all maritime activity on the Potomac River will be halted on Inauguration Day, a handful of Mall-goers will sail from Virginia to Washington on water taxis. Some people will cross the Potomac River via water taxi on Inauguration Day. Working closely with the United States Coast Guard, the Potomac Riverboat Company, based in Alexandria, Virginia, plans to ferry up to 3,200 passengers from across the frigid Potomac on seven climate-controlled boats. The service is partially a response to the closure of all bridges from Virginia to D.C. on Inauguration Day, a measure that prompted an uproar among Virginia residents. According to maritime authorities in charge of the region, PRC is the only company being allowed to taxi across the river on the 20th. "Because the taxi service provided us with a security plan that we examined and deemed adequate to provide good security, I granted them a waiver to operate at an increased security level," National Capitol Region Port Captain Brian Kelley says. "The taxis are going to operate on a strict schedule and a strict route." The Coast Guard established a temporary security zone on waterways in the National Capitol Region, stepping up restrictions day-by-day leading up to 11 p.m. on January 19. At that point, all vessels must be docked and only boats with an approved sail plan will be allowed to operate. John Lake, a ship captain and the general manager of the company, said the sail plan he submitted was approved only a week ago and details nearly every move taxis will make. "All the departures are scheduled times. And those departures are supposed to leave on-time," Lake said. "We have to call in on each departure to the Coast Guard, let them know we're preparing to get under way, and get the permission, basically, to get under way." The boats depart the Alexandria Marina for the 40-minute trip beginning around 6 a.m. and must be docked on the southwest D.C. shore by 10 a.m. From there, it's a cold, mile-long walk to the Mall, so Lake has some advice for passengers. "Show up early to get through the security check and dress warm," he said. "It's going to be nice and toasty on the boat, but not so much outside." Return trips, tentatively scheduled for around 6 p.m., are not allowed to depart D.C. until after the inaugural parade events have concluded and President Obama is secured. In keeping with the Coast Guard's security measures, Lake says all passengers must arrive at least an hour early for a full screening. Passengers that want to stay in D.C. after the early evening departures will have to find other transport back across the Potomac. PRC Vice President Charlotte Hall says tickets went on sale Monday and the initial response from customers has been enthusiastic.

# Water Taxis Navigate Choppy Waters of Inauguration Security

**WASHINGTON** — As the nation's capital braces for heightened security ahead of the presidential inauguration, water taxi operators along the Potomac are adjusting to a maze of new restrictions that have complicated one of the region's more scenic commuting options.

Captain Elena Torres, who has piloted water taxis between National Harbor and the Wharf for six years, said this year's security perimeter has forced her company to rework routes with little notice.

"Normally we've got flexibility—we can adjust for weather, for tides, whatever," Torres said, standing on the deck of her vessel as it idled near a temporary checkpoint. "This week, we're getting fairway restrictions we've never seen before. There are stretches of river that are essentially frozen for us during specific windows tied to motorcade movements and the swearing-in ceremony itself."

Torres said her crews received revised navigation charts just 48 hours before the inauguration, marking off temporary no-wake zones and security buffers extending several hundred yards from key shoreline installations.

"We're used to being nimble on the water. This is different—this is coordination with agencies that don't operate on our timeline," she said.

The Coast Guard, which oversees maritime security during major national events, confirmed that Sector Maryland-National Capital Region has implemented a series of moving safety zones synced to the inaugural schedule.

"Our job is to balance public safety with keeping commerce and transportation moving as much as possible," said Coast Guard Petty Officer First Class Daniel Whitfield, a public affairs officer with the sector. "We understand water taxis are a vital transit option for residents and visitors, so we've worked with operators to identify windows when transits can continue safely."

Whitfield said the Coast Guard deployed additional small boat crews and established real-time communication channels with commercial operators to minimize disruptions.

"We're not trying to shut the river down," he said. "We're trying to manage it so that when there's an elevated risk period—say, during movements near the Capitol or the Mall—we can clear that space quickly and then reopen it."

Still, the adjustments have meant longer wait times and occasional cancellations for passengers. Torres said her company added extra staff at docks to explain delays to travelers unfamiliar with the security protocols.

"Most people get it," she said. "They know it's a big day, a big security operation. But it does mean if you're planning to catch a water taxi during the ceremony window, build in extra time—or maybe just watch the parade instead."

# Virginia Residents Turn to Waterways as D.C. Bridges Close for Inauguration

**Washington (CNN)** — With all bridges connecting Virginia to the nation's capital shut down ahead of Monday's presidential inauguration, some enterprising Virginia residents are taking an unconventional route into the city: by boat.

Security officials announced late last week that all vehicular and pedestrian bridges spanning the Potomac River would be closed starting Sunday evening as part of an unprecedented security perimeter surrounding the National Mall. The closures, which affect major crossings including the Memorial, Key, and Arlington Memorial bridges, are intended to prevent unauthorized access to the heavily fortified inauguration zone.

For thousands of Virginia commuters and inauguration attendees who had planned to walk or drive into D.C., the announcement sent scrambling residents searching for alternatives — and some found their answer on the water.

"We've had way more inquiries about river transport in the last 48 hours than I've ever seen," said Mark Feldman, owner of a small boat rental operation in Alexandria. "People are coming to us asking if we can get them across the Potomac. It's honestly kind of amazing."

Feldman said his marina has fielded calls from residents as far as Fairfax and Loudoun counties, all hoping to secure a spot on a boat that could ferry them to docking points near the Mall.

## A Scramble for Alternatives

Local marinas and boat clubs in Alexandria, Old Town, and along the Virginia side of the Potomac report a surge in interest from residents determined not to let bridge closures derail their inauguration plans. Several marina operators say they're organizing informal shuttle services, while others note that private boat owners have offered to carry neighbors and coworkers across the river for free.

"It's kind of become a community effort," said Diane Alvarez, a longtime Alexandria resident who owns a small motorboat. "My neighbor asked if I could take her and her husband across Monday morning, and now I've got five people counting on me. I feel like I'm running a ferry service at this point."

City officials in Alexandria and Arlington have not officially sanctioned the informal boat transport but say they are aware of the workaround and have not discouraged it, provided operators follow standard maritime safety protocols.

The Coast Guard, which will maintain a restricted security zone on the Potomac during the inauguration, confirmed that recreational boat traffic will still be permitted in designated areas outside the immediate perimeter around the Mall, though vessels will be subject to inspection and monitoring.

"We understand people are looking for creative solutions," a Coast Guard spokesperson said in a statement. "Our priority is ensuring that any water traffic near the security zone is conducted safely and lawfully."

## Not Without Challenges

Boating into the district isn't without its complications. Temperatures are expected to hover near freezing Monday morning, and river conditions could prove challenging for smaller vessels. Some residents also note that docking points near the Mall remain limited, forcing boaters to walk significant distances once ashore — through the same security checkpoints as everyone else.

"It's not exactly a shortcut," said Feldman. "You still have to go through security once you're on land. But at least you're not stuck on the wrong side of a bridge."

Despite the obstacles, many Virginia residents say they're determined to witness history, bridge closures or not.

"We've talked about this for weeks — how are we going to get in?" said Alvarez. "And when we realized the boat was really our best option, honestly, it started to feel kind of fitting. Getting to the inauguration the hard way, on the water, just like people used to have to do it long before there were bridges at all."

## Security Rationale

Officials have defended the sweeping bridge closures as a necessary measure given the scale of the event and heightened security concerns. Law enforcement agencies, including the Secret Service and U.S. Park Police, have been coordinating for months on a security plan that includes tens of thousands of personnel, extensive fencing, and tightly controlled access points throughout the district.

"The safety of everyone attending — and the security of the event itself — remains our top priority," said a Secret Service spokesperson. "We recognize these measures create inconvenience, and we appreciate the public's patience and cooperation."

As Monday approaches, it remains unclear just how many Virginians will ultimately make their way across the Potomac by boat. But for those determined to attend, the river has become an unlikely — and increasingly popular — answer to a very modern problem.

*CNN's coverage of the inauguration will continue throughout the weekend as security preparations continue across the district.*
